演奏時先將一張紙緊貼梳子，再把嘴唇貼在紙上，對著梳子與紙發聲或唱出音調。聲音使紙: To play, first stretch a sheet of paper tight against a comb, then press your lips to the paper and sound or sing a note into the comb and the paper. The sound sets the paper vibrating and changes the timbre. A beginner can first practise holding the paper in place and keeping the lips sealed against it, then try changing the way they sound and watch how the paper vibrates and the sound changes.
演奏者以嘴唇壓住貼於梳齒上的紙張，再向紙張發聲；人聲使紙張振動，因而改變音色。其: The player presses the lips against the paper laid over the comb's teeth and sounds into the paper; the voice makes the paper vibrate and so alters the timbre. The sound comes from the voice and the paper's vibration added together; the volume follows how strongly the player sounds, and both range and melody depend on the voice. Compared with the other instruments in the singing-membrane class, the comb and paper is built from comb teeth and paper, but it sounds on the same principle: a membrane set moving by the human voice.

紙梳是一種簡易樂器，由梳子與貼在梳子上的紙片組成。演奏者將嘴唇貼住紙片，對著梳子: The comb and paper is a simple instrument made from a comb and a piece of paper laid over it. The player presses the lips to the paper and sings or sounds into the comb; the voice sets the paper vibrating and colours the voice. It belongs to the singing-membrane class, Hornbostel–Sachs number 241. In 1911 the Encyclopaedia Britannica called it 'the nursery's comb music', and it has also served as an improvised instrument, used to accompany country-western dances.
紙梳曾作為即興樂器，用於伴奏鄉村西部舞蹈；在爵士樂場合，蒙城藍吹奏者樂團的雷德·: The comb and paper has served as an improvised instrument to accompany country-western dances; in jazz settings Red McKenzie of the Mound City Blue Blowers played on a comb and tissue paper. In popular music it is used on the Beatles' 'Lovely Rita', Jimi Hendrix's 'Crosstown Traffic' and Graham Nash's 'Sleep Song', and on the album Hold That Tiger by the Muddy Waters band. The film Three Colours: White and British talent shows also contain demonstrations in which 'Eye of the Tiger' and 'The Final Countdown' are played on a comb and tissue paper.

You play by pressing your lips to the paper and sounding, so that the paper vibrates and the timbre changes. The source mentions that some players use thin paper, but the material of the comb itself, the exact kind and thickness of the paper, and the materials of the other parts are not stated, so nothing further can be said.
紙梳的早期文獻見於1911年《大英百科全書》，被稱為「搖籃梳樂」，歸入歌唱膜鳴樂: The earliest literature on the comb and paper is the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which calls it 'cradle comb music' and classes it among singing membranophones. Playing it is sometimes called blue-blowing, possibly in reference to the jazz group the Mound City Blue Blowers; between 1923 and 1936 Red McKenzie played on a comb and tissue paper. The comb and paper has also served as an improvised instrument for accompanying country-western dances. It later entered popular recordings, film and television, for instance the Beatles' song 'Lovely Rita', Jimi Hendrix's 1968 single 'Crosstown Traffic' and Graham Nash's 1971 'Sleep Song'.
